Spot Markets for AI Inference

Spot Markets for AI Inference

Quanyan Zhu
8 November 2026
Abstract

Inference providers size their accelerator fleets for the interactive peak and sell spare capacity through fixed discounts, such as batch tiers at half price. However, inference differs from conventional cloud capacity in four respects: capacity depends on the latency tier through batching, moving weights between models is slow and costly, spot demand can wait until its deadline, and power can bind. In this paper, we develop a framework for dynamic capacity allocation and pricing of AI inference on a shared accelerator fleet. We consider a provider that serves several models under a power cap and sells each model in an interactive tier with a speed promise and in a spot tier for preemptible work with a deadline. In each period, the provider chooses how many replicas of each model to keep loaded and what spot price to quote. We show that one interactive token displaces a fixed number ρm>1\rho_{m}>1 of spot tokens, and that the optimal spot price lies midway between the interactive price and the effective cost of capacity in the deadline window, which is close to the prevailing half price only when the fleet is slack. We further show that a spot tier raises the optimal reliability of the interactive tier, and that placement should follow persistent demand shifts while prices absorb transients. Building on these results, we design a model predictive controller based on a linear program with explicit approximation bounds, which solves each period in milliseconds. Numerical experiments on a simulated week with a measured daily demand profile, a flash crowd, and a grid curtailment show that the controller raises profit by 7.4%7.4\% over fixed half-price practice, captures 93%93\% of the gain available with perfect forecasts, keeps the interactive promise through both events, and leaves spot buyers better off.

1  Introduction

Generative AI is increasingly delivered as a metered service. When a person, an application, or an autonomous agent submits a request to a foundation model, the model produces its response one token at a time on a fleet of specialized accelerators, and the provider charges for the tokens consumed [49, 10]. As foundation models become embedded in search, software development, customer service, and multi-step agentic workflows, the production of tokens, known as inference, has emerged as a central economic activity of the AI industry. Inference is also intensive in both capital and energy. The accelerators that perform inference are among the most expensive assets in computing, and the data centers that house them have become a rapidly growing source of electricity demand [37, 17]. Therefore, the allocation and pricing of inference capacity is not only an engineering question of throughput and latency but also an economic question about the use of a scarce, costly, and perishable resource.

Inference capacity differs from a conventional commodity in three respects. First, it is perishable. An accelerator-hour that is not used to generate tokens cannot be stored and sold later, and hence idle capacity is a cost that is never recovered. Second, it is slow to reconfigure. To serve a model, a provider must load the model’s weights, often tens to hundreds of gigabytes, onto one or more accelerators, which takes from seconds to minutes and interrupts production on those accelerators [13]. Third, the quantity of capacity depends on the quality of service that it delivers. Serving systems process many requests together in a batch [45, 19], and a larger batch produces more tokens per second in total but fewer for each request [30]. As a result, a provider that promises interactive users a fast stream of tokens must keep its batches small and accept a lower throughput than the same hardware could deliver for work that can tolerate delay.

These properties shape how inference is provisioned and sold today. Interactive demand follows the working day of its users. Since weights cannot be loaded quickly enough to meet a sudden surge, providers size their fleets for the busiest hour with a margin for forecast error. Consequently, a substantial part of the fleet idles for much of the day. The major providers have responded by selling deferrable work at a discount. Batch interfaces complete requests within a day at half the standard price, flex tiers offer lower prices in exchange for slower or less reliable service, and some providers have charged less in off-peak hours [26, 4, 15, 27, 9]. One important feature shared by these offers is that their prices are fixed. In other words, the prices do not respond to whether the fleet is busy or idle, and access is rationed through rate limits and queues rather than through prices.

At the same time, the conditions under which inference capacity is supplied are becoming more variable. The release of a new model can raise demand for it sharply within hours. Agents, evaluation suites, and data pipelines generate large volumes of work that can wait minutes or hours for an answer. Moreover, data centers are increasingly constrained by their connections to the power grid, and grid operators are asking large loads to reduce consumption at short notice [17, 25]. A fixed discount cannot respond to any of these conditions. When the fleet is slack, a fixed discount may be close to the right price. When the fleet is tight, however, it leaves the scarcity value of capacity unpriced, and when the grid is stressed, it provides no signal that would move flexible work to other hours. Nevertheless, a dynamic alternative is not straightforward to design. The provider must decide which models to keep loaded and at what price to sell spare capacity before it observes the next period’s interactive load, and it must honor the deadlines of the work that it has already accepted.

Infrastructure clouds faced a related problem when they began to sell idle virtual machines. Spot instances, introduced in 2009, offered spare capacity at a price that varied with its availability [1, 3], and a body of work has studied how a data-center operator can adapt its capacity, and in spot markets also its prices, to changing demand [18, 46, 21]. However, inference differs from virtual machines in ways that change the structure of the control problem. Two of these differences have been noted above. The capacity of a replica depends on the latency tier that it serves, and moving accelerators between models is slow and costly, even though dividing a model’s replicas between tiers is a free setting of the batch scheduler. Two further differences arise from the nature of demand and supply. Spot work has a deadline rather than a start time, so demand can wait while capacity cannot. In addition, power, not only the number of accelerators, can limit production. Section 2 explains each of these features in more detail.

In this paper, we develop a framework for dynamic capacity allocation and pricing of AI inference on a shared accelerator fleet. We consider a provider that serves several models under a power cap and sells each model in two tiers: an interactive tier, at a posted price with a guaranteed decode speed, and a spot tier, for preemptible work that must be completed within a deadline, at a price that the provider may revise every period. In each period, the provider decides how many replicas of each model to keep loaded and what spot price to quote before the period’s interactive load is realized. The resulting problem is a constrained stochastic control problem with two time scales, a queue with deadlines, and coupling across models through the shared fleet and the power cap. We first study simplified versions of the problem that admit closed-form characterizations, and we then solve the full problem by model predictive control. Figure 1 illustrates the setting and its translation into control-theoretic terms.

The contributions of this paper are fourfold. First, we show that continuous batching induces a latency exchange rate between the two tiers. At the margin, one interactive token per second displaces ρm>1\rho_{m}>1 spot tokens per second, where ρm\rho_{m} is the ratio of a replica’s full-load throughputs at the two tiers’ batch caps (Lemma 1). This result converts the latency premium of interactive service into a linear capacity constraint that can be priced.

Second, we characterize optimal spot prices. On a shared fleet, the optimal spot price lies midway between the interactive price and the full marginal cost of a spot token, which includes the shadow rents of the fleet and of power. These rents are determined by water-filling across models, and hence a demand surge on one model raises the spot prices of all models (Proposition 1). When the fleet is slack, the rule reproduces the half-price discount observed in practice, and a fixed discount loses little. When the fleet is tight, however, a fixed discount forgoes the scarcity rent (Proposition 2). When work can be deferred, the relevant cost is that of the cheapest capacity within the deadline window (Theorem 1).

Third, we establish two structural results on reliability and placement. A spot tier acts as a salvage market for the safety capacity of the interactive tier and therefore raises the optimal reliability of interactive service (Theorem 2). Moreover, placement exhibits an inaction band determined by the round-trip cost of loading and unloading a model. In other words, transient shocks are absorbed by prices, and only persistent shifts justify moving weights (Theorem 3).

Fourth, we design a model predictive controller that embeds these results. A piecewise-linear approximation of revenue, tangent cuts on the expected interactive overflow, and a cumulative representation of deadlines reduce each period’s planning problem to a linear program with explicit approximation bounds (Lemmas 2 and 3). The program solves in about 77 milliseconds (Section 6).

We evaluate the controller on a simulated week of a 512512-accelerator fleet serving three models, with a daily demand profile measured on a public inference marketplace, a flash crowd triggered by a model launch, and a curtailment requested by the grid operator (Section 7). Relative to a strong version of current practice, the controller raises profit by 7.4%7.4\% and captures 93%93\% of the gain available to a controller with perfect forecasts. It keeps the interactive speed promise through both events, serves more spot work, and increases the surplus of spot buyers. Note that the sources of the gain differ across regimes. On ordinary days, the gain comes mainly from prices, whereas during the two events it comes from reallocating accelerators and power across models. Collectively, these results suggest that a spot tier with dynamic prices is more than a channel for selling idle capacity. It also serves as an instrument for managing the reliability of interactive service, absorbing demand shocks, and offering flexibility to the power grid.

The rest of the paper is organized as follows. Section 2 describes how inference capacity is produced and sold and states the problem. Section 3 reviews related work. Section 4 presents the model, and Section 5 characterizes optimal policies in simplified settings. Section 6 develops the model predictive controller, and Section 7 reports the numerical study. Section 8 discusses implications and limitations, and Section 9 concludes the paper. Proofs are collected in Appendix A.

2  Background and problem statement

In this section, we describe how inference capacity is produced and sold, explain why a substantial part of it idles, and identify the features that distinguish its allocation from that of conventional cloud capacity. We conclude the section with a statement of the problem studied in the rest of the paper. Figure 1 summarizes the setting pictorially and restates the problem in the vocabulary of stochastic control for readers who are familiar with the methods but new to AI inference.

Production of inference.

A provider serves a model by loading a copy of its weights, called a replica, onto one or more accelerators. A small dense model may fit on a single accelerator, whereas a large mixture-of-experts model may span eight or more. A request is processed in two phases. In the prefill phase, the replica reads the prompt and builds a key–value cache that summarizes it. In the decode phase, it generates the response one token at a time, and each token requires a pass through the whole model. Note that, for the batch sizes used in interactive service, a decode step is limited by memory bandwidth rather than arithmetic, since it must read the weights and the caches of all sequences in progress [30]. Therefore, serving systems process many sequences together so that one pass over the weights advances every sequence in the batch by one token. With continuous batching, sequences join and leave the batch at every step [45], and paged memory management allows the caches of many sequences to share the accelerator’s memory [19]. A larger batch raises the total throughput of a replica but slows every sequence in it, since each step takes longer. In other words, the batch size is an operating point on a trade-off between throughput and latency, and it is bounded above by the memory available for caches. Section 4.1 formalizes this trade-off.

Fleet sizing for the peak.

Interactive demand follows the working day of its users. On one public inference marketplace, the hourly token volume over 30 days has a peak-to-trough ratio of 2.62.6 across the hours of the day [32]. Since weights cannot be loaded quickly enough to meet a surge, a provider must keep enough replicas loaded to serve interactive traffic at its busiest hour with a margin for forecast error. A fleet sized for the peak of this profile runs at 69%69\% utilization on average, and at 63%63\% with a 10% safety margin. In the fleet simulated in Section 7, mean interactive load occupies 49%49\% of the accelerators on average, ranging between 33%33\% and 68%68\% over the day. The remaining accelerators represent capacity that the provider has already paid for. Note that accelerators are expensive to own or lease, and an accelerator-hour that is not used cannot be recovered later.

Fixed discounts for spare capacity.

The major providers sell deferral through batch interfaces that complete work within a day at half the standard price [26, 4, 15]. Some providers also sell flex tiers, which may be slower or unavailable at busy times, and priority tiers, which cost more [27, 5]. One provider has charged lower prices in off-peak hours [9]. Across the tiered endpoints listed on one large model router on 31 October 2026, the median flex price is 0.500.50 of the standard price of the same model and provider, the median priority price is 2.002.00, and the median batch price is 0.500.50 [28]. These ratios are round numbers set by policy. They do not change when the fleet is busy or idle, and batch tiers ration access with rate limits and queues rather than with prices. Moreover, secondary venues on which inference capacity is resold quote prices well below list [31, 41]. This situation resembles the early market for cloud capacity before spot instances priced spare virtual machines according to their availability [1, 3].

Distinctive features of inference capacity.

Dynamic pricing of spare capacity is well established for virtual machines. However, four features of inference change the control problem.

  1. 1.

    Capacity depends on the service tier. A replica’s throughput rises with its batch size, and the latency promise of the interactive tier caps the batch. Hence, the same replica produces more spot tokens than interactive tokens, and one interactive token displaces ρm>1\rho_{m}>1 spot tokens (Lemma 1). In contrast, a virtual machine is a fixed unit of capacity regardless of what it is sold as.

  2. 2.

    Placement is slow and costly, while splitting between tiers is free. Moving an accelerator from one model to another requires loading tens to hundreds of gigabytes of weights, which takes seconds for a small model and minutes for a large one [13]. In contrast, dividing a model’s replicas between interactive and spot work is a setting of the batch scheduler [45, 19]. As a result, the control problem has two time scales.

  3. 3.

    Demand can be stored, but capacity cannot. Spot work has a deadline rather than a start time, and hence admitted work waits in a backlog. The backlog is a state variable, and the right price for spot work in the current period depends on the capacity that will be free before its deadline.

  4. 4.

    Power, not only accelerators, can bind. Inference facilities are increasingly limited by their grid connections, and grid operators are asking large loads to curtail at short notice [37, 17, 25]. Spot work is the part of the load that can be curtailed without breaking a promise, as long as its deadlines can still be met.

Significance of the problem.

The problem is important for three reasons. First, the stakes are large. Accelerator fleets are among the most expensive assets in computing, and hence a few percentage points of their utilization represent substantial value. Second, the problem is becoming more pressing. Much of the work that agents and data pipelines generate, such as evaluations, synthetic data, document processing, and overnight agent runs, does not need an answer within seconds. In addition, data centers are becoming the loads that grid operators ask to flex [17, 25]. Third, a spot price that reflects the scarcity of capacity carries information beyond a single transaction. It tells buyers when flexible work is cheap to run, informs the facility of how much load it can shed when the grid is stressed, and provides a reference price on which forward contracts, capacity reservations, and other instruments for inference capacity can be written. In contrast, a fixed discount conveys none of this information.

3  Related work

In this section, we review related work on cloud spot markets, language-model serving, revenue management, electricity markets, model predictive control, and AI economics.

Spot markets for cloud capacity.

Spot instances sell the idle capacity of an infrastructure cloud at a price that varies with its availability. Agmon Ben-Yehuda et al. [1] have found that early spot prices were not always set by an open market, and Amazon Web Services later replaced bidding with smoothed prices [3]. On the provider’s side, our previous work [46] has formulated capacity allocation and pricing for the spot markets of an infrastructure cloud as a constrained optimal control problem solved by model predictive control, and Zhang et al. [47] have studied dynamic service placement across data centers with reconfiguration costs. We adopt the receding-horizon architecture of this line of work but change the plant: capacity depends on the service tier through batching, demand can wait in a backlog with deadlines, capacity changes have explicit costs, and power is a constraint. Our provider sets prices openly as a monopolist of its own spare capacity, and Remark 1 gives its competitive ask. On the buyer’s side of a spot market, Miao et al. [24] serve language models on preemptible instances.

Serving language models.

Continuous batching [45], paged key–value caches [19], chunked prefill [2], and disaggregated prefill and decode [48, 29] raise the throughput of a replica and make the throughput–latency trade-off explicit, as analyzed by Pope et al. [30]. Our batching law and the exchange rate ρm\rho_{m} summarize this trade-off for the controller. AlpaServe [20] places models on a shared cluster to exploit statistical multiplexing, and ServerlessLLM [13] reduces the cost of loading a model. These systems decide placement for a given demand. In contrast, we add prices and a deferrable tier, and we treat loading time and cost as frictions whose economic effect is characterized by Theorem 3.

Revenue management and peak-load pricing.

Selling a perishable capacity to price-sensitive demand is the problem of revenue management [14, 40]. One key difference in our setting is that the capacity regenerates every period, its size is a decision, and it is shared across products at a rate that depends on the product. Peak-load pricing [38, 8] explains why the price of capacity should rise when it is scarce. Proposition 1 is a monopoly version with several products sharing one plant, and Theorem 1 adds storable demand. The backfill theorem is a newsvendor result [6] in which the spot tier serves as the salvage market for safety capacity.

Electricity markets and data-center flexibility.

Spot pricing of electricity over space and time [7, 39, 44] provides the model for pricing a non-storable good from a constrained network. Data centers can shift workload in time to follow electricity prices or carbon intensity [33, 43, 34] and reduce their demand during grid peaks [22]. Dynamic right-sizing turns servers off when load is low and faces the same switching costs as our placement problem [21]. Lookahead control of data centers goes back at least to Kusic et al. [18]. Our contribution to this line of work is to price the flexibility. The spot tier is the curtailable part of the load, and its price tells buyers when curtailment is likely.

Model predictive control.

Receding-horizon control of constrained systems has a mature theory [23, 35]. We use it as a practical method and do not claim stability or optimality guarantees for the closed loop. Instead, the numerical study measures how close it comes to a controller with perfect forecasts. Note that the inaction bands of Theorem 3 are the discrete-time analog of those in investment under adjustment costs [11, 12].

The economics of AI inference.

Demirer et al. [10] document the pricing, supply, and demand of language-model inference, and in Zhu [49], we have studied the economics of tokens, computation, and pricing in foundation models. These studies take the provider’s capacity and costs as given or focus on posted prices. In contrast, this paper takes the provider’s side. We derive the cost of capacity from the fleet, its batching, and its power supply, and we show what spot price a provider should quote as a result.

4  The model

In this section, we present the model of the fleet, the demand, and the dynamics, and we formulate the provider’s control problem. We divide time into control periods t=0,1,…t=0,1,\dots of length Δ\Delta seconds, and we set Δ=15\Delta=15 minutes in the numerical study. Within a period, the set of loaded replicas is fixed, but the scheduler can change, at every decode step, which sequences share a batch. Therefore, the model has two layers: a slow layer of placement, decided at the start of each period, and a fast layer of batching inside the period, which we summarize by its throughput.

Placement and batching correspond to layers 2 and 3 of Fig. 2, which places them within a broader view of the provider’s operations, from the hardware at the bottom to the buyers at the top. Capacity is built up from the accelerators through the deployments, the serving engine, and the queues, and it is sold as products and tiers to buyers whose demand responds to price and latency. For each layer, the figure indicates its time scale and the elements of the model that represent it. Two features of the figure deserve emphasis. First, changing a deployment, which requires loading weights and warming caches, is a transition within layer 2 rather than a layer of its own; the model captures it through the loading time LmL_{m} and the costs κm±\kappa^{\pm}_{m}. Second, the controller acts on only two layers, the placement and the spot price, and it observes the others.

4.1  Fleet, models, and batching

Consider a provider that operates a fleet of GG identical accelerators in one facility with a power cap of WtW_{t} kilowatts. The provider serves a set ℳ={1,…,M}\mathcal{M}=\{1,\dots,M\} of models. A replica of model mm refers to one loaded copy of its weights, and it occupies gmg_{m} accelerators (e.g., one accelerator for a small dense model and eight for a large mixture-of-experts model).

Decode.

We adopt a first-order model of memory-bound decode [30]. In each step, a replica reads its weights once and the key–value cache of every sequence in its batch. Hence, a decode step of a replica that holds a batch of bb sequences takes

τm​(b)=τ0,m+τ1,m​b,0≤b≤Bm,\tau_{m}(b)=\tau_{0,m}+\tau_{1,m}\,b,\qquad 0\leq b\leq B_{m}, (1)

where τ0,m\tau_{0,m} denotes the time to stream the weights, τ1,m\tau_{1,m} the per-sequence cost of attention and cache traffic, and BmB_{m} the largest batch whose key–value caches fit in memory. Since every sequence in the batch advances one token per step, each stream runs at 1/τm​(b)1/\tau_{m}(b) tokens per second, and the replica produces θm​(b)=b/τm​(b)\theta_{m}(b)=b/\tau_{m}(b) tokens per second. Note that the throughput θm\theta_{m} is increasing and concave in bb.

Two tiers.

The provider sells two service tiers for each model.

  1. (1)

    The interactive tier promises every stream a decode speed of at least smIs^{\mathrm{I}}_{m} tokens per second. It is sold at a posted price πm\pi_{m} per token, and its demand is exogenous in the short run.

  2. (2)

    The spot tier promises completion within a deadline and a much lower speed floor sS<smIs^{\mathrm{S}}<s^{\mathrm{I}}_{m} (or none). Spot work is preemptible, i.e., the provider may pause it at any step. Its price pm,tp_{m,t} is set every period.

The speed floors cap the batch. A replica that holds any interactive stream can run batches of at most bmI=min⁡{Bm,(1/smI−τ0,m)/τ1,m}b^{\mathrm{I}}_{m}=\min\{B_{m},(1/s^{\mathrm{I}}_{m}-\tau_{0,m})/\tau_{1,m}\} sequences, whereas a replica that holds only spot work can run batches of up to bmS=min⁡{Bm,(1/sS−τ0,m)/τ1,m}b^{\mathrm{S}}_{m}=\min\{B_{m},(1/s^{\mathrm{S}}-\tau_{0,m})/\tau_{1,m}\}. We write

θmI=θm​(bmI),θmS=θm​(bmS),ρm=θmS/θmI≥1\theta^{\mathrm{I}}_{m}=\theta_{m}(b^{\mathrm{I}}_{m}),\qquad\theta^{\mathrm{S}}_{m}=\theta_{m}(b^{\mathrm{S}}_{m}),\qquad\rho_{m}=\theta^{\mathrm{S}}_{m}/\theta^{\mathrm{I}}_{m}\ \geq 1

for the full-load throughputs of a replica in the two modes and their ratio. We assume that smI<1/τ0,ms^{\mathrm{I}}_{m}<1/\tau_{0,m} so that interactive service is feasible.

Lemma 1 (Co-batching and the latency exchange rate).

Assume that replicas are divisible. Let n>0n>0 replicas of model mm carry an interactive load of r∈[0,θmI​n]r\in[0,\theta^{\mathrm{I}}_{m}n] tokens per second. Then, the largest spot throughput compatible with the interactive speed floor is

κm​(n,r)=θmS​n−ρm​r.\kappa_{m}(n,r)=\theta^{\mathrm{S}}_{m}\,n-\rho_{m}\,r. (2)

It is attained by running r/θmIr/\theta^{\mathrm{I}}_{m} replicas at batch bmIb^{\mathrm{I}}_{m} with interactive streams only and the remaining n−r/θmIn-r/\theta^{\mathrm{I}}_{m} replicas at batch bmSb^{\mathrm{S}}_{m} with spot streams only. With whole replicas, running k=⌈r/θmI⌉k=\lceil r/\theta^{\mathrm{I}}_{m}\rceil replicas at batch bmIb^{\mathrm{I}}_{m} and filling their spare slots with spot streams yields a spot throughput of at least κm​(n,r)−(θmS−θmI)\kappa_{m}(n,r)-(\theta^{\mathrm{S}}_{m}-\theta^{\mathrm{I}}_{m}).

Proof. See Appendix A.2.

Lemma 1 converts the latency premium of interactive service into an exchange rate between the tiers. In other words, at the margin, one interactive token per second displaces ρm\rho_{m} spot tokens per second. When neither batch cap is set by memory, ρm=(1−τ0,m​sS)/(1−τ0,m​smI)\rho_{m}=(1-\tau_{0,m}s^{\mathrm{S}})/(1-\tau_{0,m}s^{\mathrm{I}}_{m}). In the calibration of Section 7, the spot batch is set by memory, and ρm\rho_{m} is 1.24, 1.51, and 1.40 for the small, medium, and large models, respectively (Tables 1 and 3). The lemma also shows that the split of a model’s replicas between the tiers costs nothing to change. This split is a scheduler setting rather than a placement decision, and hence the controller can leave it to the batch scheduler inside the period.

4.2  Demand

Interactive load.

Let Rm,tR_{m,t} denote the average rate, in tokens per second, at which interactive traffic for model mm arrives during period tt. This rate is random, and the provider forecasts it with mean r^m,t\hat{r}_{m,t} and standard deviation σm,t\sigma_{m,t} (Section 6.1). Each interactive token that is served earns πm\pi_{m}. A token that cannot be served at the promised speed is lost and incurs a penalty βm\beta_{m} in service credits and goodwill.

Spot demand.

In period tt, a population of spot buyers for model mm would buy Λm,t\Lambda_{m,t} tokens of work at a price of zero. Their valuations per token are uniform on [0,πm][0,\pi_{m}], so that no buyer pays more for deferrable service than the interactive price at which it could buy immediate service. At spot price pp, the work admitted is

am,t=Λm,t​(1−p/πm)+,equivalentlyp=πm​(1−am,t/Λm,t).a_{m,t}=\Lambda_{m,t}\,(1-p/\pi_{m})^{+},\qquad\text{equivalently}\qquad p=\pi_{m}\,(1-a_{m,t}/\Lambda_{m,t}). (3)

Linear demand is a common choice in the pricing of cloud capacity [46]. It keeps the pricing rules in closed form, and its slope αm,t=Λm,t/πm\alpha_{m,t}=\Lambda_{m,t}/\pi_{m} scales with the size of the buyer population. Note that spot revenue a​πm​(1−a/Λm,t)a\,\pi_{m}(1-a/\Lambda_{m,t}) is a concave quadratic in the admitted volume, while every constraint of the model is linear in it. Therefore, we optimize over admissions and recover the price from the demand curve.

Deadlines.

Work admitted in period tt must be completed by the end of period t+D−1t+D-1. Work that misses its deadline expires, its price is refunded, and the provider pays a penalty γm\gamma_{m} per token. This convention matches current batch interfaces, which do not charge for requests that expire [26]. While admitted work waits, the provider incurs a small holding cost hmh_{m} per token per period, which captures the buyers’ preference for earlier completion and breaks ties in favor of serving early. The deadline DD is a contract term. For example, D=1D=1 corresponds to a spot tier with no deferral, D=8D=8 (two hours) is in the range of current flex tiers, and D=96D=96 (a day) corresponds to a batch tier.

4.3  Dynamics, power, and costs

Placement.

Let nm,t≥0n_{m,t}\geq 0 denote the number of replicas of model mm loaded in period tt. These replicas must fit in the fleet:

∑mgm​nm,t≤G.\textstyle\sum_{m}g_{m}\,n_{m,t}\leq G. (4)

Loading a replica takes LmL_{m} seconds of weight transfer and warm-up, during which its accelerators produce nothing. Let um,t=(nm,t−nm,t−1)+u_{m,t}=(n_{m,t}-n_{m,t-1})^{+} denote the loads and vm,t=(nm,t−1−nm,t)+v_{m,t}=(n_{m,t-1}-n_{m,t})^{+} the unloads. Then, the replicas that are effective in period tt are

n~m,t=nm,t−ℓm​um,t,ℓm=Lm/Δ.\tilde{n}_{m,t}=n_{m,t}-\ell_{m}\,u_{m,t},\qquad\ell_{m}=L_{m}/\Delta. (5)

Each load also incurs a direct cost κm+\kappa^{+}_{m}, and each unload incurs a cost κm−\kappa^{-}_{m} for the in-flight sequences that it drains and the caches that it discards. Accelerators that hold no model are parked.

Service.

Interactive traffic has priority. The provider serves Ym,t=min⁡{Rm,t,θmI​n~m,t}Y_{m,t}=\min\{R_{m,t},\theta^{\mathrm{I}}_{m}\tilde{n}_{m,t}\} tokens per second, and the overflow Om,t=Rm,t−Ym,tO_{m,t}=R_{m,t}-Y_{m,t} is lost. By Lemma 1, the remaining spot capacity of the period is

Km,t=Δ⁡(θmS​n~m,t−ρm​Ym,t)tokens.K_{m,t}=\Delta\,\bigl(\theta^{\mathrm{S}}_{m}\tilde{n}_{m,t}-\rho_{m}Y_{m,t}\bigr)\ \ \text{tokens}. (6)

Spot work is served in first-in-first-out order. Let qm,tq_{m,t} denote the backlog at the start of period tt, xm,t≤Km,tx_{m,t}\leq K_{m,t} the spot work served, and zm,tz_{m,t} the work that expires. Then,

qm,t+1=qm,t+am,t−xm,t−zm,t.q_{m,t+1}=q_{m,t}+a_{m,t}-x_{m,t}-z_{m,t}. (7)

Since all spot work of model mm has the same relative deadline, first-in-first-out is also earliest-deadline-first. This property allows us to write the deadlines as linear constraints on cumulative service (Lemma 2).

Power and energy.

A loaded but idle accelerator draws w0w^{0} kW, a parked accelerator draws wpark<w0w^{\mathrm{park}}<w^{0}, and decode at full load adds w1w^{1}. Power rises in proportion to the share of a replica’s capacity in use, and hence the facility draws

Ωt=wpark​G+∑mgm​[(w0−wpark)​nm,t+w1​(Ym,tθmI+xm,tΔ​θmS)]≤Wt.\Omega_{t}=w^{\mathrm{park}}G+\sum_{m}g_{m}\Bigl[(w^{0}-w^{\mathrm{park}})\,n_{m,t}+w^{1}\Bigl(\frac{Y_{m,t}}{\theta^{\mathrm{I}}_{m}}+\frac{x_{m,t}}{\Delta\theta^{\mathrm{S}}_{m}}\Bigr)\Bigr]\ \leq W_{t}. (8)

Note that a replica at full load draws gm​(w0+w1)g_{m}(w^{0}+w^{1}) in either mode. Electricity costs ete_{t} dollars per kWh. Both the price ete_{t} and the cap WtW_{t} may change at short notice (e.g., when the grid operator calls a demand-response event).

Profit.

The profit of period tt is given by

Jt=∑m[Δ​πm​Ym,t+pm,t​am,t−refundsm,t−γm​zm,t−Δ​βm​Om,t−hm​qm,t+1−κm+​um,t−κm−​vm,t]−Δ3600​et​Ωt,J_{t}=\sum_{m}\Bigl[\Delta\pi_{m}Y_{m,t}+p_{m,t}a_{m,t}-\text{refunds}_{m,t}-\gamma_{m}z_{m,t}-\Delta\beta_{m}O_{m,t}-h_{m}q_{m,t+1}-\kappa^{+}_{m}u_{m,t}-\kappa^{-}_{m}v_{m,t}\Bigr]-\frac{\Delta}{3600}\,e_{t}\,\Omega_{t}, (9)

where refunds are the prices paid for the expiring work zm,tz_{m,t}. Since accelerators are owned or leased for much longer than a period, their cost is sunk and does not appear in (9). Instead, it enters the analysis through the shadow price of the fleet constraint (4).

4.4  The control problem

At the start of period tt, the provider knows the history up to t−1t-1, namely, past loads, the backlog with its deadlines, and the replicas in place. It also knows the announced electricity prices and power caps. The provider then chooses the placement nt=(nm,t)mn_{t}=(n_{m,t})_{m} and the spot prices pt=(pm,t)mp_{t}=(p_{m,t})_{m}. Afterwards, interactive load RtR_{t} and the spot intercepts Λt\Lambda_{t} are realized, interactive traffic is served, and the spot backlog is served within the remaining capacity and power. The provider’s problem is formulated as

maxnon-anticipative ​(nt,pt)⁡𝔼⁡[∑t=0T−1Jt]subject to (3)–(8).\max_{\text{non-anticipative }(n_{t},p_{t})}\ \mathbb{E}\Bigl[\sum_{t=0}^{T-1}J_{t}\Bigr]\quad\text{subject to \eqref{eq:demand}--\eqref{eq:power}}. (P)

Figure 4 illustrates the feedback loop. Problem (P) is a constrained stochastic control problem. Its state, which includes the replicas, the backlog by deadline, and the forecast state, is too large for exact dynamic programming. Moreover, its controls interact through the shared fleet and power cap, and its dynamics have two time scales. Therefore, Section 5 first studies deterministic and one-period versions of the problem to learn what optimal policies look like, and Section 6 then solves (P) by model predictive control.

5  Structure of optimal policies

In this section, we study four simplified versions of (P). Each version isolates one feature of the inference setting, namely, a shared fleet whose capacity depends on the tier, storable demand, random interactive load, and costly placement. The results explain the behavior of the controller of Section 6, and they provide the provider with pricing rules that can be published.

Throughout this section, we let λte=et​Δ/3600\lambda^{e}_{t}=e_{t}\Delta/3600 denote the cost of drawing one kW for one period, and we let

w^=w0−wpark+w1\hat{w}=w^{0}-w^{\mathrm{park}}+w^{1}

denote the power that a fully loaded accelerator draws in excess of a parked one.

5.1  One period: shadow prices of a shared fleet

Consider a single period in which interactive load RmR_{m} and the spot intercept Λm\Lambda_{m} are known, spot work must be served within the period (D=1D=1), and the previous placement does not matter (no loading cost). The provider chooses placement and spot admissions by solving

maxn,a≥0\displaystyle\max_{n,a\geq 0} ∑m[am​πm​(1−amΛm)−λe​(gm​(w0−wpark)​nm+w1​gm​(RmθmI+amΔ​θmS))]\displaystyle\sum_{m}\Bigl[a_{m}\pi_{m}\Bigl(1-\frac{a_{m}}{\Lambda_{m}}\Bigr)-\lambda^{e}\Bigl(g_{m}(w^{0}-w^{\mathrm{park}})n_{m}+w^{1}g_{m}\Bigl(\frac{R_{m}}{\theta^{\mathrm{I}}_{m}}+\frac{a_{m}}{\Delta\theta^{\mathrm{S}}_{m}}\Bigr)\Bigr)\Bigr] (10)
s.t.\displaystyle\text{s.t. } am≤Δ⁡(θmS​nm−ρm​Rm)(m∈ℳ),∑mgm​nm≤G[ν],Ω≤W[η].\displaystyle a_{m}\leq\Delta(\theta^{\mathrm{S}}_{m}n_{m}-\rho_{m}R_{m})\ \ (m\in\mathcal{M}),\qquad\sum_{m}g_{m}n_{m}\leq G\ \ [\nu],\qquad\Omega\leq W\ \ [\eta].

We assume that interactive load alone fits, i.e., ∑mgm​Rm/θmI≤G\sum_{m}g_{m}R_{m}/\theta^{\mathrm{I}}_{m}\leq G, and that the power it draws, with every replica it needs loaded, is at most WW. For each model, we define the full marginal cost of a spot token as

𝑀𝐶m​(ν,η)=gm​[ν+(λe+η)​w^]Δ​θmS.\mathit{MC}_{m}(\nu,\eta)=\frac{g_{m}\bigl[\nu+(\lambda^{e}+\eta)\,\hat{w}\bigr]}{\Delta\,\theta^{\mathrm{S}}_{m}}. (11)

In other words, this quantity is the cost of one replica-period, which consists of the fleet’s shadow rent ν\nu per accelerator plus the energy and the shadow price of power at full load, divided by the spot tokens that the replica-period produces.

Proposition 1 (Spot prices on a shared fleet).

Problem (10) has an optimal solution with multipliers ν≥0\nu\geq 0 for the fleet and η≥0\eta\geq 0 for power such that:

  1. (i)

    Spot prices. Model mm sells spot work if and only if 𝑀𝐶m<πm\mathit{MC}_{m}<\pi_{m}, and then its spot price and volume are

    pm=12​(πm+𝑀𝐶m),am=12​Λm​(1−𝑀𝐶m/πm).p_{m}=\tfrac{1}{2}\bigl(\pi_{m}+\mathit{MC}_{m}\bigr),\qquad a_{m}=\tfrac{1}{2}\Lambda_{m}\bigl(1-\mathit{MC}_{m}/\pi_{m}\bigr). (12)
  2. (ii)

    Interactive opportunity cost. At the margin, an interactive token costs ρm​𝑀𝐶m\rho_{m}\mathit{MC}_{m}. For every model with Rm>0R_{m}>0, −Δ​ρm​𝑀𝐶m-\Delta\rho_{m}\mathit{MC}_{m} is a supergradient of the optimal profit with respect to RmR_{m}: one more token per second of interactive load reduces the period’s profit by at least Δ​ρm​𝑀𝐶m\Delta\rho_{m}\mathit{MC}_{m}, and by exactly that wherever the optimal profit is differentiable in RmR_{m}.

  3. (iii)

    Water-filling. Suppose that the power cap is slack at the solution described here, so that η=0\eta=0. Let

    N⁡(ν)=∑mgm​[RmθmI+Λm2​Δ​θmS​(1−𝑀𝐶m​(ν,0)πm)+]N(\nu)=\sum_{m}g_{m}\Bigl[\frac{R_{m}}{\theta^{\mathrm{I}}_{m}}+\frac{\Lambda_{m}}{2\Delta\theta^{\mathrm{S}}_{m}}\Bigl(1-\frac{\mathit{MC}_{m}(\nu,0)}{\pi_{m}}\Bigr)^{+}\Bigr]

    denote the number of accelerators that the provider would use at shadow rent ν\nu. Then, ν=0\nu=0 if N⁡(0)≤GN(0)\leq G; otherwise, ν\nu is the unique solution of N⁡(ν)=GN(\nu)=G.

  4. (iv)

    Spillovers. When η=0\eta=0, ν\nu is nondecreasing in every Rm′R_{m^{\prime}} and Λm′\Lambda_{m^{\prime}}. Hence, every model’s spot price is nondecreasing, and its spot volume nonincreasing, in the interactive load and spot demand of every other model.

  5. (v)

    Slack fleet. If neither the fleet nor power binds, pm=12​πm+12​gm​λe​w^/(Δ​θmS)p_{m}=\frac{1}{2}\pi_{m}+\frac{1}{2}g_{m}\lambda^{e}\hat{w}/(\Delta\theta^{\mathrm{S}}_{m}): half the interactive price, plus half the energy cost of a spot token.

Proof. See Appendix A.3.

Part (v) offers an interpretation of current practice. When the fleet is slack, the monopoly price for spare capacity is half the interactive price, up to a negligible energy term (Table 1). This is exactly the 50% discount that current batch tiers charge [26, 4, 15]. Note that the result depends on the assumption that valuations are uniform up to the interactive price, and hence it should not be interpreted as a structural law. Nevertheless, it does indicate where a fixed half-price rule goes wrong, namely, when the fleet is tight. In this case, ν>0\nu>0, and the optimal spot price rises above half the interactive price by 12​gm​ν/(Δ​θmS)\frac{1}{2}g_{m}\nu/(\Delta\theta^{\mathrm{S}}_{m}). Part (iv) shows that this happens for every model at once since the models share the fleet. For example, a launch-day surge on the large model raises the spot price of the small one, even though no small-model buyer has changed its behavior. Virtual machine types in a cloud spot market share a data center in the same way. One key difference is that the rate at which one virtual machine type displaces another is fixed by the machine size, whereas here it depends on the latency tier through ρm\rho_{m}. Therefore, part (ii) also gives the provider a pricing floor for its interactive tier, i.e., πm≥ρm​𝑀𝐶m\pi_{m}\geq\rho_{m}\mathit{MC}_{m}.

Proposition 2 (What a fixed discount loses).

Fix one model and one period, and let cc denote the marginal cost of a spot token, including any shadow price of capacity at the optimum. Let p∗p^{\ast} denote the optimal spot price and p¯\bar{p} any other price.

  1. (i)

    If capacity binds at neither price, the loss from charging p¯\bar{p} is Λπ​(p¯−p∗)2\frac{\Lambda}{\pi}(\bar{p}-p^{\ast})^{2}. Over periods t=1,…,Tt=1,\dots,T in which this holds, a fixed price p¯\bar{p} loses ∑tαt​(p¯−pt∗)2≥(∑tαt)​Varα​(p∗)\sum_{t}\alpha_{t}(\bar{p}-p^{\ast}_{t})^{2}\ \geq\ \bigl(\sum_{t}\alpha_{t}\bigr)\,\mathrm{Var}_{\alpha}(p^{\ast}), where αt=Λt/π\alpha_{t}=\Lambda_{t}/\pi and Varα\mathrm{Var}_{\alpha} is the α\alpha-weighted variance of the optimal price path.

  2. (ii)

    If capacity KK binds at the optimum, so that p∗p^{\ast} is the market-clearing price, a lower price p¯<p∗\bar{p}<p^{\ast} with admissions rationed to KK loses (p∗−p¯)​K(p^{\ast}-\bar{p})\,K, i.e., the whole scarcity rent on the gap.

Proof. See Appendix A.4.

Therefore, the loss from a fixed discount is second order in slack periods and first order in tight periods. In other words, a half-price rule is close to optimal when there is spare capacity, whereas in tight periods it gives up the full scarcity rent while rate limits ration access. Figure 5 illustrates both regimes on the calibrated fleet. The same asymmetry underlies the classical case for peak-load pricing [38, 8], and it has been noted for flat-rate charging of cloud capacity, which is inefficient both when demand is far below capacity and when it exceeds capacity [46].

5.2  Deferral: prices follow the cheapest capacity in the window

Spot demand can be stored since work can wait until its deadline, whereas capacity cannot. To understand the effect of this asymmetry on prices, we fix the placement of one model so that spot capacities KtK_{t} are given for t=0,…,T−1t=0,\dots,T-1, and we assume that demand is known. The provider solves

max⁡∑ta,x≥0⁡[at​π​(1−atΛt)−ct​xt−h​qt+1]s.t. ​xt≤Kt​[μt],(7) with ​z≡0,deadline ​D,\max_{a,x\geq 0}\ \sum_{t}\Bigl[a_{t}\pi\Bigl(1-\frac{a_{t}}{\Lambda_{t}}\Bigr)-c_{t}x_{t}-h\,q_{t+1}\Bigr]\quad\text{s.t. }x_{t}\leq K_{t}\ [\mu_{t}],\ \eqref{eq:backlog}\text{ with }z\equiv 0,\ \text{deadline }D, (13)

where ctc_{t} is the energy cost of a spot token, q0=0q_{0}=0, and all work must be served by its deadline. Let 𝒲t={t,…,min⁡(t+D,T)−1}\mathcal{W}_{t}=\{t,\dots,\min(t+D,T)-1\} denote the service window of work admitted in period tt.

Theorem 1 (Deferral pricing).

Problem (13) has an optimal solution with capacity multipliers μt≥0\mu_{t}\geq 0 such that, with the effective cost

Ct=minτ∈𝒲t⁡[cτ+μτ+h⁡(τ−t)],C_{t}=\min_{\tau\in\mathcal{W}_{t}}\bigl[c_{\tau}+\mu_{\tau}+h(\tau-t)\bigr], (14)
  1. (i)

    every period with at>0a_{t}>0 has spot price pt=12​(π+Ct)p_{t}=\frac{1}{2}(\pi+C_{t}), and every period with at=0a_{t}=0 has Ct≥πC_{t}\geq\pi;

  2. (ii)

    work admitted in period tt can be scheduled so that it is served only in periods that attain the minimum in (14);

  3. (iii)

    if capacity is slack in some period τ∈𝒲t\tau\in\mathcal{W}_{t} (μτ=0\mu_{\tau}=0), then pt≤12​(π+cτ+h⁡(τ−t))p_{t}\leq\frac{1}{2}\bigl(\pi+c_{\tau}+h(\tau-t)\bigr);

  4. (iv)

    optimal profit is nondecreasing in DD.

Proof. See Appendix A.6.

Theorem 1 shows that a buyer who accepts a DD-period deadline buys the cheapest capacity in its window, valued at the shadow price of that later period plus the cost of waiting for it, and that the provider passes half of the saving on in the price. With D=1D=1, Ct=ct+μtC_{t}=c_{t}+\mu_{t}, and the spot price follows the current scarcity, as in Proposition 1. With a longer deadline, a peak-hour price is capped by an off-peak cost (part iii, Fig. 6). In other words, deferral flattens spot prices and moves the scarcity rent from peak periods to the slack periods that absorb the deferred work. Hence, a deadline is a product attribute with a price. A buyer who is willing to wait buys capacity that would otherwise idle, and the provider shares the saving through a lower price for longer deadlines.

5.3  Backfill: spot work makes reliability cheaper

Placement is chosen before interactive load is known since weights take time to load. Therefore, a provider that wants interactive streams to meet their speed floor must hold safety capacity, which idles unless it is put to other use. Spot work provides such a use. Consider one model in one period with interactive load RR drawn from a continuous distribution FF, F¯=1−F\bar{F}=1-F. The provider chooses nn replicas at cost k>0k>0 each (the fleet’s shadow rent plus static energy), serves min⁡(R,θI​n)\min(R,\theta^{\mathrm{I}}n) interactive tokens per second, and sells the spot capacity left over by Lemma 1, which is worth v≥0v\geq 0 per token at the margin. Its expected profit is given by

Φ⁡(n)=Δ⁡[(π+β)​𝔼​min⁡(R,θI​n)−β​𝔼​R+v​θS​𝔼​(n−RθI)+]−k​n.\Phi(n)=\Delta\Bigl[(\pi+\beta)\,\mathbb{E}\min(R,\theta^{\mathrm{I}}n)-\beta\,\mathbb{E}R+v\,\theta^{\mathrm{S}}\,\mathbb{E}\Bigl(n-\frac{R}{\theta^{\mathrm{I}}}\Bigr)^{\!+}\Bigr]-k\,n. (15)
Theorem 2 (Spot backfill raises the optimal service level).

Assume that ρ​v<π+β\rho v<\pi+\beta (an interactive token is worth more than the spot capacity it displaces) and k<Δ​θI​(π+β)k<\Delta\theta^{\mathrm{I}}(\pi+\beta). Then Φ\Phi is concave, and:

  1. (i)

    if Δ​θS​v≥k\Delta\theta^{\mathrm{S}}v\geq k, Φ\Phi is nondecreasing, i.e., spot work alone pays for the replica, and nn is set by the fleet;

  2. (ii)

    otherwise, the optimal n∗n^{\ast} satisfies the critical-fractile condition

    ℙ⁡(R>θI​n∗)=ϖ⁡(v):=k/(Δ​θI)−ρ​v(π+β)−ρ​v;\mathbb{P}\bigl(R>\theta^{\mathrm{I}}n^{\ast}\bigr)=\varpi(v):=\frac{k/(\Delta\theta^{\mathrm{I}})-\rho v}{(\pi+\beta)-\rho v}; (16)
  3. (iii)

    ϖ⁡(v)\varpi(v) is strictly decreasing in vv. The optimal probability of missing the interactive speed floor falls as spot capacity becomes more valuable. Without a spot market (v=0v=0), it is the newsvendor fractile k/(Δ​θI​(π+β))k/(\Delta\theta^{\mathrm{I}}(\pi+\beta));

  4. (iv)

    if R∼N⁡(r^,σ2)R\sim N(\hat{r},\sigma^{2}), then n∗=(r^+z∗​σ)/θIn^{\ast}=(\hat{r}+z^{\ast}\sigma)/\theta^{\mathrm{I}} with z∗=ΦN−1​(1−ϖ⁡(v))z^{\ast}=\Phi_{N}^{-1}(1-\varpi(v)), where ΦN\Phi_{N} and ϕN\phi_{N} are the standard normal distribution and density functions. The expected spot capacity is Δ​ρ​σ​(z∗​ΦN​(z∗)+ϕN​(z∗))\Delta\rho\,\sigma\,\bigl(z^{\ast}\Phi_{N}(z^{\ast})+\phi_{N}(z^{\ast})\bigr), which grows with the volatility σ\sigma of interactive load.

Proof. See Appendix A.7.

The economics are those of the classic newsvendor [6], but the salvage value of unused capacity is now provided by the spot market. When the spot market is liquid (vv high), safety capacity is cheap to hold since whatever the interactive tier does not use is sold. Therefore, a provider with a spot tier should promise, and deliver, better interactive service than one without (Fig. 7a). Amazon’s spot instances sell the unused part of a fleet sized for on-demand and reserved customers in the same way [1]. One key difference for inference is that the unused capacity is mostly the safety margin of the interactive tier, and its size grows with the volatility of interactive demand (part iv). This is the mechanism by which the controller of Section 6 sizes placements, since its expected-overflow constraints embed (16).

5.4  Placement: pricing transients and placing trends

Moving accelerators between models is slow and costly, whereas changing a spot price is instant and free. To isolate this trade-off, we decompose (P) by pricing the shared fleet. Given rents for accelerators and power, the value of holding nn replicas of model mm in period tt is a function Vt​(n)V_{t}(n), defined as the optimal value of that period’s pricing and service problem net of the rents. This function is concave in nn since that problem is a concave program in which nn enters only through linear terms (Lemma A.1 in Appendix A.1). The placement problem of one model is then given by

max⁡∑t=0T−1n0,…,nT−1⁡[Vt​(nt)−κ+​(nt−nt−1)+−κ−​(nt−1−nt)+],n−1​ given.\max_{n_{0},\dots,n_{T-1}}\ \sum_{t=0}^{T-1}\Bigl[V_{t}(n_{t})-\kappa^{+}(n_{t}-n_{t-1})^{+}-\kappa^{-}(n_{t-1}-n_{t})^{+}\Bigr],\qquad n_{-1}\text{ given}. (17)
Theorem 3 (Placement hysteresis).

Let each Vt:ℝ→ℝV_{t}:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R} be concave.

  1. (i)

    For any optimal plan n∗n^{\ast}, there are supergradients wt∈∂Vt​(nt∗)w_{t}\in\partial V_{t}(n^{\ast}_{t}) such that the continuation value ξt=∑s=tT−1ws\xi_{t}=\sum_{s=t}^{T-1}w_{s} satisfies ξt∈[−κ−,κ+]\xi_{t}\in[-\kappa^{-},\kappa^{+}] for all tt, with ξt=κ+\xi_{t}=\kappa^{+} whenever nt∗>nt−1∗n^{\ast}_{t}>n^{\ast}_{t-1} and ξt=−κ−\xi_{t}=-\kappa^{-} whenever nt∗<nt−1∗n^{\ast}_{t}<n^{\ast}_{t-1}.

  2. (ii)

    Consequently, if a replica is loaded in period t1t_{1} and the next change is an unload in period t2t_{2}, then ∑s=t1t2−1ws=κ++κ−\sum_{s=t_{1}}^{t_{2}-1}w_{s}=\kappa^{+}+\kappa^{-}, i.e., the marginal replica earns exactly its round-trip switching cost over its tenure. Over any window [t1,t2)[t_{1},t_{2}), |∑s=t1t2−1ws|≤κ++κ−\bigl|\sum_{s=t_{1}}^{t_{2}-1}w_{s}\bigr|\leq\kappa^{+}+\kappa^{-}.

  3. (iii)

    (Spike absorption.) Let n¯\bar{n} maximize a concave VV, n−1=n¯n_{-1}=\bar{n}, and Vt=VV_{t}=V except on a set SS of dd periods, on which the value of replicas beyond n¯\bar{n} rises by at most δ≥0\delta\geq 0 each: Vt​(n)−Vt​(n¯)≤V⁡(n)−V⁡(n¯)+δ​(n−n¯)+V_{t}(n)-V_{t}(\bar{n})\leq V(n)-V(\bar{n})+\delta\,(n-\bar{n})^{+} for all nn. If d​δ≤κ+d\,\delta\leq\kappa^{+}, the constant plan nt≡n¯n_{t}\equiv\bar{n} is optimal. If plans must end at n¯\bar{n}, the same holds whenever d​δ≤κ++κ−d\,\delta\leq\kappa^{+}+\kappa^{-}.

Proof. See Appendix A.8.

Part (iii) provides the operational rule, and Fig. 8 illustrates it. A transient that raises the marginal value of an extra replica by δ\delta per period for dd periods is not worth a reload when d​δd\delta is below the round-trip cost. In this case, the provider absorbs the transient with the fast lever. The spot price rises (Proposition 1(iv)), spot work is preempted and deferred within its deadline (Theorem 1), and interactive traffic keeps its speed. Only persistent shifts, such as a regional daily cycle or a launch that lasts for hours, justify moving weights. For large models, whose weights take minutes to load and whose replicas span many accelerators, κ±\kappa^{\pm} is large, and the band of inaction is wide. Note that modeling switching through explicit load and unload costs, rather than a quadratic penalty on capacity changes, yields the inaction bands familiar from investment under adjustment costs [11, 12].

Remark 1 (Price-taking providers).

Suppose that the provider sells spot capacity on a competitive exchange, where it can sell up to A¯t\bar{A}_{t} tokens at a price ptexp^{\mathrm{ex}}_{t} that it does not control. The revenue term at​π​(1−at/Λt)a_{t}\pi(1-a_{t}/\Lambda_{t}) of (13) then becomes ptex​atp^{\mathrm{ex}}_{t}a_{t}, with at≤A¯ta_{t}\leq\bar{A}_{t}. At an optimum, with CtC_{t} defined by (14) at the optimal multipliers, the provider sells the full depth A¯t\bar{A}_{t} when ptex>Ctp^{\mathrm{ex}}_{t}>C_{t} and nothing when ptex<Ctp^{\mathrm{ex}}_{t}<C_{t}. Therefore, it behaves as a seller whose ask equals its effective cost CtC_{t}, with no markup. The monopoly markup 12​(π−Ct)\frac{1}{2}(\pi-C_{t}) in Proposition 1 and Theorem 1 is thus what market power adds to this ask.

Proof. See Appendix A.9.

6  Model predictive control

In this section, we develop the model predictive controller. The controller applies the receding-horizon principle of model predictive control [23, 35], which has been used to manage data centers and cloud capacity [18, 46]. At the start of every period, the controller forecasts demand over the next HH periods, solves a deterministic program over that horizon, applies the first period’s placement and prices, and repeats the procedure one period later with new information. Three features distinguish the program from those used for virtual machine capacity. First, the program has to handle a queue with deadlines. Second, the random interactive load enters through its expected overflow rather than its mean. Third, capacity changes carry explicit costs rather than a quadratic penalty. All three features can be expressed with linear constraints, and hence each period’s problem is a linear program that solves in milliseconds.

6.1  Forecasts

For k=0,…,H−1k=0,\dots,H-1 steps ahead, the controller requires forecasts r^m,t+k\hat{r}_{m,t+k} and σm,t+k\sigma_{m,t+k} of the mean and standard deviation of interactive load, a forecast Λ^m,t+k\hat{\Lambda}_{m,t+k} of the spot intercept, and the electricity prices and power caps that the grid operator has announced. In the numerical study, interactive load is a seasonal profile R¯m,t\bar{R}_{m,t} times a multiplicative deviation, i.e., Rm,t=R¯m,t​(1+ϵm,t)R_{m,t}=\bar{R}_{m,t}(1+\epsilon_{m,t}), where ϵ\epsilon is a first-order autoregression with coefficient ϕ\phi and stationary standard deviation ς\varsigma. The controller estimates the current deviation from the last observed load and forecasts

r^m,t+k=R¯m,t+k​(1+ϕk+1​ϵ^m,t−1),σm,t+k=R¯m,t+k​ς​1−ϕ2​(∑i=0kϕ2​i)1/2.\hat{r}_{m,t+k}=\bar{R}_{m,t+k}\bigl(1+\phi^{k+1}\hat{\epsilon}_{m,t-1}\bigr),\qquad\sigma_{m,t+k}=\bar{R}_{m,t+k}\,\varsigma\sqrt{1-\phi^{2}}\,\Bigl(\sum_{i=0}^{k}\phi^{2i}\Bigr)^{1/2}. (18)

As a result, a flash crowd, which the seasonal profile does not contain, enters the forecast as a deviation that is expected to decay at rate ϕ\phi. The controller learns about a grid event when the operator announces it, which is 22 hours ahead in the study. Note that any forecaster can replace (18) since the program below needs only the means and standard deviations.

6.2  The planning program

Fix the current period tt and index the horizon by k=0,…,H−1k=0,\dots,H-1. We write r^m,k\hat{r}_{m,k} for r^m,t+k\hat{r}_{m,t+k}, and similarly for the other forecasts. For every model and step, the decision variables are the replicas nm,kn_{m,k}, loads um,ku_{m,k}, and unloads vm,kv_{m,k}; the expected interactive service ym,ky_{m,k} and overflow om,ko_{m,k} in tokens per second; the spot admissions am,ka_{m,k}, service xm,kx_{m,k}, and expiries zm,kz_{m,k} in tokens; and a power shortfall ωk\omega_{k} that keeps the program feasible when an announced cap cannot be met. The effective replicas are n~m,k=nm,k−ℓm​um,k\tilde{n}_{m,k}=n_{m,k}-\ell_{m}u_{m,k} as in (5).

Π^K(a)=max{∑j=1Kπm(1−2​j−1K)aj:∑jaj=a, 0≤aj≤Λ^/K}.\hat{\Pi}_{K}(a)=\max\Bigl\{\sum_{j=1}^{K}\pi_{m}\Bigl(1-\frac{2j-1}{K}\Bigr)a^{j}\ :\ \sum_{j}a^{j}=a,\ 0\leq a^{j}\leq\hat{\Lambda}/K\Bigr\}. (19)
