where Ωk\Omega_{k} is the power (8) with YY replaced by yy, nm,−1n_{m,-1} is the current placement, dm,kd_{m,k} is the part of the current backlog that falls due by step kk, and cωc^{\omega} is a large penalty for drawing more than the cap. The objective is the expected profit (9) with the exogenous interactive revenue Δ​πm​r^m,k\Delta\pi_{m}\hat{r}_{m,k} dropped. In this objective, each token of overflow loses its price and incurs its penalty. Similarly, expired work loses its price, which is refunded, and incurs its penalty. The last three lines of constraints represent the deadlines, the availability of work, and a terminal condition that the horizon end with an empty backlog, which prevents the controller from pushing work beyond the horizon.

Lemma 2 (Deadlines as cumulative constraints).

Fix one model, admissions a0,…,aH−1a_{0},\dots,a_{H-1}, and an initial backlog in which dkd_{k} units fall due by step kk. Serve the backlog in first-in-first-out order. A sequence of service and expiry (xk+zk)k(x_{k}+z_{k})_{k} is feasible and completes every unit by its deadline if and only if, for every kk, cumulative service lies between the work due and the work available:

dk+∑j≤k−D+1aj≤∑j≤k(xj+zj)≤q0+∑j≤kaj.d_{k}+\sum_{j\leq k-D+1}a_{j}\ \leq\ \sum_{j\leq k}(x_{j}+z_{j})\ \leq\ q_{0}+\sum_{j\leq k}a_{j}.

Proof. See Appendix A.5.

Lemma 2 uses the fact that all spot work of a model has the same relative deadline so that first-in-first-out order is also earliest-deadline-first order. With heterogeneous deadlines, the same constraints hold for each deadline class, and the controller would need one queue per class.

Lemma 3 (Approximation error).
  1. (i)

    Π^K\hat{\Pi}_{K} is the piecewise-linear interpolation of Π⁡(a)=π​a​(1−a/Λ^)\Pi(a)=\pi a(1-a/\hat{\Lambda}) at the points a=j​Λ^/Ka=j\hat{\Lambda}/K, and 0≤Π⁡(a)−Π^K​(a)≤π​Λ^/(4​K2)0\leq\Pi(a)-\hat{\Pi}_{K}(a)\leq\pi\hat{\Lambda}/(4K^{2}) on [0,Λ^][0,\hat{\Lambda}]. The error is at most 1/K21/K^{2} of the largest revenue π​Λ^/4\pi\hat{\Lambda}/4, which is 0.062%0.062\% for K=40K=40.

  2. (ii)

    The right-hand side of (20), maximized over ii, is at most the expected overflow and equals it at the grid points. Between grid points zi<zi+1z_{i}<z_{i+1}, the gap is at most σ​(zi+1−zi)2​ϕN​(0)/4\sigma(z_{i+1}-z_{i})^{2}\phi_{N}(0)/4, and for the grid used it is at most 0.0031​σ0.0031\,\sigma on the grid’s range.

Proof. See Appendix A.10.

Therefore, the program slightly understates spot revenue and slightly understates the risk of interactive overflow. Neither error matters at the resolution of the study. The planned price is obtained from the demand curve at the planned admissions, i.e., pm,t=πm​(1−am,0/Λ^m,0)p_{m,t}=\pi_{m}(1-a_{m,0}/\hat{\Lambda}_{m,0}). Since the optimal admissions usually sit at a breakpoint of Π^K\hat{\Pi}_{K}, prices move in ticks of πm/K\pi_{m}/K, which is 2.5%2.5\% of the interactive price for K=40K=40.

6.3  The control loop

Algorithm 1 summarizes the closed loop. Two steps convert the plan into actions. First, the planned replicas are rounded to whole numbers, rounding to the nearest integer where the fleet allows and down otherwise. Second, the planned price is posted, and buyers decide how much work to submit at that price. The program learns what buyers actually submitted only in the next period, when the realized admissions appear in the backlog. Therefore, any gap between planned and realized demand is absorbed by the queue and corrected by the next plan through feedback.

Relation to the structural results of Section 5.

The program (21) contains the four simplified problems of Section 5 as special cases, and its optimality conditions reproduce their rules. For one step with D=1D=1 and no switching costs, the program reduces to (10), up to the approximations of Lemma 3, and hence its spot prices are 12​(πm+𝑀𝐶m)\frac{1}{2}(\pi_{m}+\mathit{MC}_{m}) with the shadow rent νk\nu_{k} and power price ηk\eta_{k} of that step (Proposition 1). With longer deadlines, the cumulative constraints of Lemma 2 allow work to move to the cheapest step in its window, and prices follow the effective cost CtC_{t} of Theorem 1. The cuts (20) set the interactive safety margin at the critical fractile of Theorem 2, with the spot tier as salvage value. In particular, at the optimum, the slope 1−ΦN​(z)1-\Phi_{N}(z) of the active cut balances the cost of a replica against the value of its spot capacity. Moreover, the load and unload costs produce the inaction band of Theorem 3. The multipliers μm,k\mu_{m,k}, νk\nu_{k}, and ηk\eta_{k} are also useful outputs in their own right. For example, ρm​𝑀𝐶m\rho_{m}\mathit{MC}_{m} is a floor for interactive prices, and the effective cost CtC_{t} is the provider’s competitive ask on an exchange (Remark 1).

Size and speed.

With MM models and horizon HH, the program has (8+K)​M​H+H(8+K)MH+H variables, which amounts to 2,3202,320 for M=3M=3, H=16H=16, and K=40K=40, and about 30​M​H30MH constraints, most of which are cuts. HiGHS [16] solves it in about 77 milliseconds on a laptop, compared with a control period of 1515 minutes. Fleets with tens of models and horizons of a day should remain well within the period since the program grows only linearly in both. In contrast, the cost of exact dynamic programming grows exponentially with the number of models and the length of the deadline.

7  Numerical study

In this section, we evaluate how much a provider gains from dynamic placement and pricing, where the gain comes from, and how it depends on forecasts, switching costs, and contract terms. All numbers come from the scripts listed in Appendix C.

7.1  Setup

Fleet and models.

Consider a provider that runs G=512G=512 accelerators under a nominal power cap of 380380 kW and serves three models (Table 1). The small model fits on one accelerator, the medium model on two, and the large mixture-of-experts model on eight. Their batching parameters yield interactive batch caps between 83 and 133 sequences and exchange rates ρm\rho_{m} between 1.241.24 and 1.511.51. Loading weights takes 3030, 9090, and 300300 seconds, which corresponds to 0.030.03, 0.100.10, and 0.330.33 of a 15-minute period. Each load costs $1.001.00 and each unload $0.500.50 per accelerator, which accounts for warm-up energy, drained sequences, and discarded caches. Interactive prices are $0.150.15, $0.800.80, and $3.003.00 per million tokens. An idle loaded accelerator draws 0.250.25 kW, a parked one draws 0.060.06 kW, and decode at full load adds 0.450.45 kW.

Demand.

Mean interactive load follows the hour-of-day profile of token volume on a public inference marketplace, computed from 30 days of hourly data, with a peak-to-trough ratio of 2.62.6 [32]. The medium model’s profile is shifted by eight hours, as for a second region, and the large model’s daily swing is half again as large. Weekend load is 0.910.91 of weekday load. At the mean, interactive traffic occupies 49%49\% of the fleet on average. Note that real serving traces are bursty around their daily pattern [42]. Accordingly, load deviates from its mean by a first-order autoregression with coefficient 0.900.90 and standard deviation 10%10\%, as in (18). Spot demand follows a flatter daily profile with an independent 10%10\% noise every period, and it is scaled so that, at half the interactive price, it would occupy 35%35\% of the fleet. Spot work must finish within D=8D=8 periods (120120 minutes). A lost interactive token costs βm=5​πm\beta_{m}=5\,\pi_{m} in service credits and goodwill, and an expired spot token is refunded and costs γm=0.5​πm\gamma_{m}=0.5\,\pi_{m}.

Electricity and events.

Electricity costs $0.0650.065 per kWh on average, with a daily swing of $0.0250.025 that peaks at 20:00 UTC. The simulated week contains two events that the seasonal profile does not anticipate. On Wednesday, a model launch doubles the large model’s interactive load, ramping up from 13:0013:00 UTC over 11 hour, holding for 55 hours, and decaying over 33 hours. On Friday, the grid operator calls a demand-response event. From 17:0017:00 UTC for 22 hours, the facility must stay below 62%62\% of its nominal cap (236236 kW), and electricity costs $0.800.80 per kWh. The event is announced 22 hours ahead.

Policies.

We compare six policies (Table 2). Posted represents current practice, namely, the best static placement for a typical weekday and a spot tier sold at half the interactive price. It is a strong version of that practice since the same planning program sets a rate limit on spot admissions so that the posted tier never accepts more work than it expects to finish by the deadline. Dynamic price and Dynamic placement each add one of the two levers. Myopic uses both levers with a persistence forecast, i.e., it expects current interactive load, spot demand, electricity price, and power cap to continue unchanged. MPC is Algorithm 1 with the forecasts (18) and a horizon of 1616 periods (44 hours). Oracle knows the realized future over twice that horizon and bounds what any controller could achieve with this program.

Simulation.

Each policy is run for one week at 15-minute periods on 2020 random draws of interactive load and spot demand, with the same draws for every policy. The plant serves interactive traffic first at the effective replicas (5), serves spot work first-in-first-out within the capacity (6), and enforces the power cap by shedding spot work first and interactive work second. Profit is computed by (9) without the holding cost, which serves as a planning device. Gains are measured against Posted, paired by draw, and reported with standard errors across draws.

7.2  Results

Profit gain of 7.4% from dynamic control.

Table 3 summarizes the week. MPC earns $369.8369.8 thousand, compared with $344.1344.1 thousand for Posted, which is a gain of 7.4%7.4\% (standard error 0.320.32), and it captures 93%93\% of the gain of the Oracle. Of the $25.625.6 thousand gained per week, $13.313.3 thousand comes from interactive penalties avoided, $2.72.7 thousand from interactive revenue no longer lost, and $12.212.2 thousand from additional spot revenue, while switching costs take back $1.61.6 thousand, and energy, refunds, and expiry penalties take back $0.90.9 thousand. In addition, the interactive tier receives better service. MPC misses the speed promise on 0.01%0.01\% of interactive tokens, compared with 0.25%0.25\% for Posted. Note that the two levers are complements. Dynamic prices alone gain 2.7%2.7\%, dynamic placement alone 5.2%5.2\%, and both together under the same forecasts 7.4%7.4\%. Forecasts of the daily cycle add a little. The Myopic controller gains 6.9%6.9\%, with more than half again as many accelerator loads as MPC, since it keeps reacting to the load that it has just seen.

Prices on ordinary days and placement during events.

Figure 9 breaks the gain down by day. On the five days without events, MPC gains 2.5%2.5\%, and dynamic prices alone already gain 2.4%2.4\%. On these days, the fleet is tight only for a few evening hours. As Proposition 2 predicts, the fixed discount loses little when capacity is slack, and its losses are concentrated in the tight hours. On the day of the flash crowd, MPC gains 38.4%38.4\%, and on the day of the grid event, it gains 7.4%7.4\%. Prices cannot help on these days since the interactive tier is the one short of capacity, and only moving accelerators or power to it can help. Figure 10 shows the week under MPC. Placement follows the daily cycle in small steps and moves sharply only for the two events. Spot prices stay at or within a tick or two of half price for most of the week and rise during the events.

The flash crowd.

When the large model’s load doubles, MPC moves accelerators from the medium model, whose load is low at that hour, to the large one, namely, from 216216 to 360360 accelerators at the peak, compared with a static allocation of 224224 (Fig. 11a,b). Since the forecast learns the surge from the load it observes, the first periods are served from the safety margin. In the first draw, Posted fails to serve 0.60.6 billion interactive tokens during the surge, and MPC fails to serve 0.010.01 billion. Dynamic prices alone fail to serve 0.60.6 billion, the same as Posted. The reason is that raising the spot price frees spot capacity on the large model’s replicas, but the interactive tier needs more replicas rather than more room on the ones it has. At the same time, MPC raises the spot price of every model, to 0.780.78 of the interactive price for the large model and to 0.730.73 and 0.730.73 for the small and medium ones, respectively (Fig. 11c). The other models’ prices rise because they gave up accelerators, which is the spillover of Proposition 1(iv).

The grid event.

Two hours before the event, MPC learns that the cap will fall to 236236 kW. It raises spot prices to slow admissions, serves more of the backlog before the event, and, at the start of the event, unloads replicas to park their accelerators, going from 500500 to 322322 loaded accelerators (Fig. 10b). Facility power falls by 111111 kW from its level in the two hours before (Fig. 11d). The interactive tier is served in full throughout, and the spot tier absorbs the curtailment. In particular, MPC serves 1.21.2 billion spot tokens in the two hours of the event, compared with 6.96.9 billion in the two hours before. In contrast, Posted keeps its replicas loaded, cannot fit even its interactive load under the cap, and loses 1.21.2 billion interactive tokens in the first draw (0.530.53 billion on average). The spot price during the event reaches 0.780.78 of the interactive price for the large model (Fig. 11f). In this sense, the spot tier serves as the facility’s flexible load, and its price tells buyers when the facility is curtailed.

Buyers.

Spot buyers are not worse off. Although dynamic prices are above half price in tight hours, MPC serves more spot work in total. The posted tier rations by a rate limit that is set before demand is known, and it turns work away whenever demand exceeds the limit. In contrast, a price admits whatever buyers want at that price and lets the backlog absorb the surprise. Moreover, MPC has more capacity when it is needed since it moves replicas. It serves 526526 billion spot tokens a week, compared with 495495 billion for Posted, and spot buyers’ surplus is 6.5%6.5\% higher. Profit plus buyer surplus rises by 7.3%7.3\%. The cost to buyers is a longer wait. The mean delay of a spot token rises from 1111 to 1515 minutes, and its 95th percentile rises from 3333 to 5151 minutes, which is still well within the 120120-minute deadline. Only 0.07%0.07\% of admitted spot work expires. The Oracle waits longest since it knows best when capacity will be free.

7.3  Sensitivity

In this subsection, we vary one feature at a time on 10 draws, with gains paired by draw against Posted under the same conditions (Fig. 12).

Lookahead.

A controller that plans one period ahead gains 5.5%5.5\%. Planning one hour ahead gains 6.8%6.8\%, and planning four hours ahead gains 7.1%7.1\%, with no further gain from eight hours (Fig. 12a). A few hours suffice since the deadline is two hours and placement transients last a few hours.

Switching costs and loading time.

Without switching costs, MPC gains 7.7%7.7\% but loads 7,4147,414 accelerators a week. The base cost cuts loads to 1,0981,098 for a gain of 7.1%7.1\%. As the cost rises, placement freezes (Theorem 3). At 64 times the base cost, the controller loads 66 accelerators a week and gains 2.7%2.7\%, which is the gain of dynamic prices alone (Fig. 12b). Loading time matters much less than loading cost. Scaling all load times by 0, 1, 2, and 3 yields gains of 7.2%7.2\%, 7.1%7.1\%, 7.1%7.1\%, and 7.0%7.0\%, since the controller loads ahead of need, and the lost fraction of a period matters only when a load is a surprise.

Deadlines.

Longer deadlines raise the profit of both policies (Fig. 12c), as predicted by Theorem 1(iv). With a deadline of one period, MPC earns $363.6363.6 thousand and Posted $341.0341.0 thousand; with 88 hours, they earn $371.7371.7 thousand and $350.2350.2 thousand, respectively. The gain of MPC over Posted is 6.6%6.6\% and 6.1%6.1\% at the two ends. Deferral and dynamic pricing are partial substitutes since a long deadline allows even a fixed-price tier to move work out of tight hours. This observation is consistent with current batch tiers, which pair a fixed discount with a 24-hour window.

Forecast noise.

With a standard deviation of interactive-load deviations of 5%5\%, MPC gains 7.3%7.3\% and Myopic 6.8%6.8\%. At 30%30\%, they gain 8.5%8.5\% and 7.2%7.2\%, respectively (Fig. 12d). The gain does not shrink with noise since noise hurts the static policy more. A static placement must cover the unconditional variation of load, whereas the controller re-plans every period and sizes its margin to the error of a forecast a few periods ahead, which is much smaller when deviations persist. Both sell their margins as spot capacity, as in Theorem 2.

8  Discussion

In this section, we discuss the implications of our results, their implementation, and their limitations.

Implications for providers.

Four operating rules follow from Section 5, and each of them continues to hold in the closed loop of Section 7.

  1. 1.

    Price spot work midway between the interactive price and its effective cost. The effective cost CtC_{t} is the cheapest cost of serving the work anywhere in its deadline window, including the shadow rent of the fleet and of power in that period (Theorem 1). When the fleet is slack, the resulting spot price is close to the prevailing half price (Proposition 1(v)). When the fleet is tight, the price is higher, and it is higher for every model at once since the models share the fleet.

  2. 2.

    Price interactive service above ρm​𝑀𝐶m\rho_{m}\mathit{MC}_{m}. An interactive token displaces ρm\rho_{m} spot tokens (Lemma 1), and hence the shadow cost of interactive capacity is the spot cost scaled by the latency exchange rate (Proposition 1(ii)). A provider that prices its fast tiers off its standard tier by a fixed multiple ignores the scarcity of the fleet.

  3. 3.

    Hold more safety capacity when a spot tier can use it. Spot work serves as the salvage market for the interactive tier’s safety margin, and hence the optimal probability of missing the speed promise falls as the spot tier becomes more valuable (Theorem 2). In other words, the spot tier and the interactive tier’s reliability are complements rather than rivals.

  4. 4.

    Price the transients and place the trends. Move weights only when the cumulative value of a replica over the expected duration of a shift exceeds the round-trip cost of loading and unloading it (Theorem 3). Absorb shorter shifts with the spot price and the backlog.

Implementation.

The controller requires forecasts of means and standard deviations, the current backlog with its deadlines, and the announced electricity prices and power caps. Its program is a linear program of a few thousand variables that solves in milliseconds, and hence it can run every few minutes alongside an existing batch scheduler. Note that the scheduler needs no change. It serves interactive traffic first and fills the remaining slots with spot work in first-in-first-out order, which is what continuous-batching servers already do with priorities. Moreover, the spot price can be published as a schedule over the next few hours, which informs buyers of when capacity is likely to be cheap and when the facility expects to curtail.

Market power and the half-price rule.

Our provider is a monopolist of its own spare capacity facing linear demand, and the factor 12\frac{1}{2} in the pricing rules comes from that demand curve. With other valuation distributions, the markup over CtC_{t} changes, but the cost side of every result does not. In particular, the shadow prices of the fleet and power, the effective cost under deferral, the critical fractile, and the inaction band are properties of the provider’s operations rather than of its demand. If the provider sold its spare capacity on a competitive exchange, it would ask CtC_{t} itself (Remark 1), and the difference between the monopoly price and CtC_{t} measures the provider’s market power over its spot tier.

The spot tier as flexible load.

Grid operators increasingly ask large new loads to curtail during the few hours a year when the grid is stressed [25]. The grid event of Section 7 shows that a spot tier makes such curtailment cheap for an inference provider. The interactive tier keeps its promise, and the curtailment falls on work whose buyers accepted a deadline and are compensated for it through a lower price. The shadow price η\eta of power in the planning program represents the provider’s value of a kilowatt at each hour. A provider could use it to bid its flexibility into a demand-response program, which would turn the spot tier’s flexibility into revenue from the grid as well as from buyers.

Limitations.

The model is a fluid model. It summarizes batching by full-load throughputs and does not track the latency of individual requests, the split between prefill and decode, or the memory of key–value caches beyond the batch cap. It treats interactive demand as exogenous in the short run and spot buyers as price-takers who do not time their submissions against the price schedule. Moreover, forecast errors are normal, and there is one facility with one kind of accelerator. The planning program is solved by receding horizon without closed-loop guarantees. In addition, the numerical study is stylized. Its daily profile is measured, but its fleet, models, prices, and events are illustrative, and hence its percentages indicate magnitudes rather than predict a provider’s results. Each of these limitations points to a direction for further work. Possible directions include several facilities with transfer between them, as in Zhang et al. [47]; prefill and decode as two resources; demand curves learned online; buyers who choose deadlines from a menu of prices; and robust or stochastic versions of the program.

9  Conclusion

Inference providers operate fleets sized for the interactive peak and sell the remaining capacity through fixed discounts. In this paper, we have developed a framework for allocating and pricing this capacity dynamically. Four features distinguish inference from conventional cloud capacity: capacity depends on the latency tier, placement is slow and costly while the split between tiers is free, demand can wait until a deadline, and power can bind. We have shown that, when these features are taken into account, the provider’s problem has a clear structure. Spot prices lie midway between the interactive price and the effective cost of capacity in the deadline window. Interactive capacity carries a shadow cost scaled by the latency exchange rate. A spot tier raises the optimal reliability of the interactive tier. Placement should follow persistent shifts in demand and leave transients to prices. Building on these elements, we have designed a model predictive controller that solves a small linear program each period. In a simulated week, the controller raises profit by 7.4%7.4\% over a fixed half-price policy, captures 93%93\% of the gain available with perfect forecasts, keeps the interactive promise through a flash crowd and a grid curtailment, and leaves spot buyers better off.

More broadly, the analysis suggests that the price of spare inference capacity should be understood as an operational signal rather than a fixed discount. This price summarizes, at each moment, the scarcity of accelerators, the cost and availability of power, and the flexibility that buyers offer through their deadlines. As inference becomes a basic input to economic activity and a significant load on the power grid, mechanisms that make this signal explicit will matter for the efficiency of AI services and for their integration with the energy system. As future work, we would extend the framework to facilities linked by transfers of work, to prefill and decode as separate resources, and to demand curves learned online. Other directions include buyers who choose deadlines strategically from a menu of prices and competition among providers whose spot tiers serve overlapping buyers.

Appendix A Proofs

In this appendix, we prove the results of Sections 4, 5 and 6. Section A.1 collects the facts that the proofs use. The proofs then follow in the order in which the results appear, except that Lemma 2 is proved before Theorem 1, which uses it, and Remark 1 is proved after Theorem 3.

A.1  Preliminaries

Supergradients and optimality conditions.

For a concave function VV on ℝ\mathbb{R}, ∂V⁡(n)={w:V⁡(m)≤V⁡(n)+w⁡(m−n)​∀m}\partial V(n)=\{w:\ V(m)\leq V(n)+w(m-n)\ \forall m\} denotes its superdifferential, which is the interval between the right and left derivatives of VV at nn. Note that all optimization problems below maximize a concave objective subject to linear constraints. For such problems, the Karush–Kuhn–Tucker (KKT) conditions, with supergradients in place of gradients where the objective is not differentiable, are necessary at an optimum without any further constraint qualification, and they are sufficient for optimality [36, Sections 28–29]. We use this fact without further mention.

With τm​(b)=τ0,m+τ1,m​b\tau_{m}(b)=\tau_{0,m}+\tau_{1,m}b and θm​(b)=b/τm​(b)\theta_{m}(b)=b/\tau_{m}(b),

θm′​(b)=τ0,mτm​(b)2>0,θm′′​(b)=−2​τ0,m​τ1,mτm​(b)3≤0,\theta_{m}^{\prime}(b)=\frac{\tau_{0,m}}{\tau_{m}(b)^{2}}>0,\qquad\theta_{m}^{\prime\prime}(b)=-\frac{2\tau_{0,m}\tau_{1,m}}{\tau_{m}(b)^{3}}\leq 0,

and hence throughput is increasing and concave in the batch size, as stated in Section 4.1. The speed of each stream, 1/τm​(b)1/\tau_{m}(b), is decreasing in bb, and therefore a speed floor ss is met exactly by the batches b≤(1/s−τ0,m)/τ1,mb\leq(1/s-\tau_{0,m})/\tau_{1,m}. Concave value functions.

The placement problem of Section 5.4 relies on the following standard fact.

Lemma A.1 (Concave value of a parametric concave program).

Let C⊆ℝp×ℝqC\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{p}\times\mathbb{R}^{q} be convex and f:C→ℝf:C\to\mathbb{R} concave. For nn in the projection NN of CC onto ℝq\mathbb{R}^{q}, let V⁡(n)=sup{f⁡(x,n):(x,n)∈C}V(n)=\sup\{f(x,n):(x,n)\in C\}. If VV is finite on NN, then VV is concave on NN.

Proof. Since ε\varepsilon is arbitrary, VV is concave. ∎

In Section 5.4, Vt​(n)V_{t}(n) is defined as the optimal value of one period’s pricing and service problem with nn replicas, net of the rents. That problem maximizes an objective that is jointly concave in its decisions and in nn (a concave quadratic revenue less linear costs) over a polyhedron in which nn enters linearly. Therefore, Lemma A.1 shows that VtV_{t} is concave, as assumed in Theorem 3.

A.5  Proof of Lemma 2 (deadlines as cumulative constraints)

We order the units of work by deadline, breaking ties by admission time. Since all work has the same relative deadline DD, this order is the order of admission, and hence first-in-first-out service removes units in this order. Let Xk=∑j≤k(xj+zj)X_{k}=\sum_{j\leq k}(x_{j}+z_{j}) denote the cumulative work removed by the end of step kk. Under first-in-first-out, the units removed by step kk are exactly the first XkX_{k} units in the order. The work due by step kk consists of the old backlog due by then, dkd_{k}, plus the work admitted at steps jj with j+D−1≤kj+D-1\leq k. Every unit due by kk is removed by kk if and only if XkX_{k} is at least this amount, which is the left inequality. The right inequality states that no more work is removed than has arrived. Conversely, any nondecreasing XX that satisfies both inequalities for all kk is realized by first-in-first-out service of Xk−Xk−1X_{k}-X_{k-1} units at step kk. ∎

(ii) If Δ​θS​v<k\Delta\theta^{\mathrm{S}}v<k, then Φ′​(n)→Δ​v​θS−k<0\Phi^{\prime}(n)\to\Delta v\theta^{\mathrm{S}}-k<0 as n→∞n\to\infty, while Φ′​(0)=Δ⁡(π+β)​θI−k>0\Phi^{\prime}(0)=\Delta(\pi+\beta)\theta^{\mathrm{I}}-k>0 when F⁡(0)=0F(0)=0, by the assumption on kk. For a load distribution with support on the whole line, such as the normal in (iv), we let nn range over ℝ\mathbb{R}, and Φ′​(n)→Δ⁡(π+β)​θI−k>0\Phi^{\prime}(n)\to\Delta(\pi+\beta)\theta^{\mathrm{I}}-k>0 as n→−∞n\to-\infty. Solving for F¯​(θI​n∗)\bar{F}(\theta^{\mathrm{I}}n^{\ast}) and dividing the numerator and the denominator by θI\theta^{\mathrm{I}} yields (16).

(iii) We write ϖ⁡(v)=(A−ρ​v)/(B−ρ​v)\varpi(v)=(A-\rho v)/(B-\rho v) with A=k/(Δ​θI)A=k/(\Delta\theta^{\mathrm{I}}) and B=π+βB=\pi+\beta. The assumption on kk is equivalent to A<BA<B, and ϖ′​(v)=ρ⁡(A−B)/(B−ρ​v)2<0\varpi^{\prime}(v)=\rho(A-B)/(B-\rho v)^{2}<0. At v=0v=0, ϖ=A/B\varpi=A/B.

A.8  Proof of Theorem 3 (placement hysteresis)

We write (17) with loads ut≥0u_{t}\geq 0 and unloads vt≥0v_{t}\geq 0, nt−nt−1=ut−vtn_{t}-n_{t-1}=u_{t}-v_{t}, and objective ∑t[Vt​(nt)−κ+​ut−κ−​vt]\sum_{t}[V_{t}(n_{t})-\kappa^{+}u_{t}-\kappa^{-}v_{t}]. At an optimum, we may take ut​vt=0u_{t}v_{t}=0 since reducing both by the same amount saves κ++κ−>0\kappa^{+}+\kappa^{-}>0. We attach a free multiplier ξt\xi_{t} to the tt-th equality and set ξT=0\xi_{T}=0. The KKT conditions are

ξt≤κ+(= if ut>0),−ξt≤κ−(= if vt>0),wt:=ξt−ξt+1∈∂Vt(nt).\xi_{t}\leq\kappa^{+}\ (=\text{ if }u_{t}>0),\qquad-\xi_{t}\leq\kappa^{-}\ (=\text{ if }v_{t}>0),\qquad w_{t}:=\xi_{t}-\xi_{t+1}\in\partial V_{t}(n_{t}).

(i) Telescoping the last condition with ξT=0\xi_{T}=0 gives ξt=∑s≥tws\xi_{t}=\sum_{s\geq t}w_{s}, and the first two conditions give the stated range and equalities.

(ii) If the replica is loaded at t1t_{1} and the next change is an unload at t2t_{2}, then ξt1=κ+\xi_{t_{1}}=\kappa^{+} and ξt2=−κ−\xi_{t_{2}}=-\kappa^{-}, and hence ∑s=t1t2−1ws=ξt1−ξt2=κ++κ−\sum_{s=t_{1}}^{t_{2}-1}w_{s}=\xi_{t_{1}}-\xi_{t_{2}}=\kappa^{+}+\kappa^{-}. For any window, |∑s=t1t2−1ws|=|ξt1−ξt2|≤κ++κ−\bigl|\sum_{s=t_{1}}^{t_{2}-1}w_{s}\bigr|=|\xi_{t_{1}}-\xi_{t_{2}}|\leq\kappa^{+}+\kappa^{-}.

(iii) By sufficiency of the KKT conditions, the constant plan nt≡n¯n_{t}\equiv\bar{n}, with u=v=0u=v=0, is optimal if there exist wt∈∂Vt​(n¯)w_{t}\in\partial V_{t}(\bar{n}) whose tail sums ξt=∑s≥tws\xi_{t}=\sum_{s\geq t}w_{s} lie in [−κ−,κ+][-\kappa^{-},\kappa^{+}]. For t∉St\notin S, 0∈∂V⁡(n¯)0\in\partial V(\bar{n}) since n¯\bar{n} maximizes VV. For t∈St\in S, the assumption and V⁡(n)≤V⁡(n¯)V(n)\leq V(\bar{n}) give Vt​(n)−Vt​(n¯)≤δ​(n−n¯)+V_{t}(n)-V_{t}(\bar{n})\leq\delta(n-\bar{n})^{+}. For n>n¯n>\bar{n}, this inequality bounds the right derivative of VtV_{t} at n¯\bar{n} by δ\delta. For n<n¯n<\bar{n}, it shows that the left derivative is nonnegative. Since the superdifferential of VtV_{t} at n¯\bar{n} is the interval between these derivatives, it contains a point wt∈[0,δ]w_{t}\in[0,\delta]. With these choices, ξt∈[0,d​δ]⊆[−κ−,κ+]\xi_{t}\in[0,d\delta]\subseteq[-\kappa^{-},\kappa^{+}] when d​δ≤κ+d\delta\leq\kappa^{+}. If plans must return to n¯\bar{n}, we add the terminal transition from nT−1n_{T-1} to nT=n¯n_{T}=\bar{n} with its own load and unload costs. Its multiplier ξT\xi_{T} is then free in [−κ−,κ+][-\kappa^{-},\kappa^{+}] instead of zero. Choosing ξT=−κ−\xi_{T}=-\kappa^{-} gives ξt∈[−κ−,−κ−+d​δ]\xi_{t}\in[-\kappa^{-},-\kappa^{-}+d\delta], which lies in [−κ−,κ+][-\kappa^{-},\kappa^{+}] when d​δ≤κ++κ−d\delta\leq\kappa^{+}+\kappa^{-}. ∎

A.9  Proof of Remark 1 (price-taking providers)

We replace the revenue as​π​(1−as/Λs)a_{s}\pi(1-a_{s}/\Lambda_{s}) in (13) by psex​asp^{\mathrm{ex}}_{s}a_{s} and add the constraints as≤A¯sa_{s}\leq\bar{A}_{s}. Since the reformulation in the proof of Theorem 1 concerns only the service of admitted work, it still applies, and the problem is equivalent to (24) with the new revenue and the depth constraints. This problem is a linear program whose feasible set is nonempty (take a=f=0a=f=0) and compact. Therefore, it has an optimum, and the KKT conditions hold with multipliers λs\lambda_{s}, μτ≥0\mu_{\tau}\geq 0, and ζs≥0\zeta_{s}\geq 0 for the depth constraints. Stationarity in asa_{s} and fs​τf_{s\tau} reads

psex−λs−ζs≤0(=0​ if ​as>0),λs−cτ−μτ−h⁡(τ−s)≤0(=0​ if ​fs​τ>0),p^{\mathrm{ex}}_{s}-\lambda_{s}-\zeta_{s}\leq 0\ \ (=0\text{ if }a_{s}>0),\qquad\lambda_{s}-c_{\tau}-\mu_{\tau}-h(\tau-s)\leq 0\ \ (=0\text{ if }f_{s\tau}>0),

and, as in the proof of Theorem 1, the second condition gives λs≤Cs\lambda_{s}\leq C_{s}, with equality if as>0a_{s}>0.

Suppose that psex>Csp^{\mathrm{ex}}_{s}>C_{s}. If as<A¯sa_{s}<\bar{A}_{s}, then ζs=0\zeta_{s}=0 by complementary slackness, and the first condition gives psex≤λs≤Csp^{\mathrm{ex}}_{s}\leq\lambda_{s}\leq C_{s}, a contradiction. Hence, as=A¯sa_{s}=\bar{A}_{s}. Suppose instead that psex<Csp^{\mathrm{ex}}_{s}<C_{s}. A.10  Proof of Lemma 3 (approximation error)

(i) The marginal revenues π⁡(1−(2​j−1)/K)\pi(1-(2j-1)/K) decrease in jj, and hence an optimal split fills the segments in order. With w=Λ^/Kw=\hat{\Lambda}/K, the value at a=j​wa=jw is π​w​∑i=1j(1−(2​i−1)/K)=π​w​(j−j2/K)=π​a​(1−a/Λ^)\pi w\sum_{i=1}^{j}(1-(2i-1)/K)=\pi w(j-j^{2}/K)=\pi a(1-a/\hat{\Lambda}), since ∑i≤j(2​i−1)=j2\sum_{i\leq j}(2i-1)=j^{2}. Between breakpoints, Π^K\hat{\Pi}_{K} is linear, and hence it is the linear interpolation of Π\Pi at the breakpoints. Since Π\Pi is concave with Π′′=−2π/Λ^\Pi^{\prime\prime}=-2\pi/\hat{\Lambda}, the interpolation lies below it, and the standard interpolation error bound gives Π⁡(a)−Π^K​(a)≤12​|Π′′|​(w/2)2=π​Λ^/(4​K2)\Pi(a)-\hat{\Pi}_{K}(a)\leq\frac{1}{2}|\Pi^{\prime\prime}|\,(w/2)^{2}=\pi\hat{\Lambda}/(4K^{2}). Divided by max⁡Π=π​Λ^/4\max\Pi=\pi\hat{\Lambda}/4, this bound equals 1/K21/K^{2}.

(ii) For R∼N⁡(r^,σ2)R\sim N(\hat{r},\sigma^{2}) and capacity cc, 𝔼​(R−c)+=σ​L​(z)\mathbb{E}(R-c)^{+}=\sigma L(z) with z=(c−r^)/σz=(c-\hat{r})/\sigma. Note that LL is convex with L′​(z)=−(1−ΦN​(z))L^{\prime}(z)=-(1-\Phi_{N}(z)). For the gap, fix consecutive grid points a=zi<b=zi+1a=z_{i}<b=z_{i+1} and z∈[a,b]z\in[a,b], and let s=(L⁡(b)−L⁡(a))/(b−a)s=(L(b)-L(a))/(b-a) denote the slope of the chord of LL between them. By convexity, LL lies below the chord on [a,b][a,b], and the chord exceeds the tangents at aa and bb by u⁡(z−a)u\,(z-a) and v⁡(b−z)v\,(b-z), where u=s−L′​(a)≥0u=s-L^{\prime}(a)\geq 0 and v=L′​(b)−s≥0v=L^{\prime}(b)-s\geq 0. Therefore, the gap between LL and the larger of the two tangents is at most

min⁡{u⁡(z−a),v⁡(b−z)}≤u​vu+v​(b−a)≤u+v4​(b−a)=(b−a)​(L′​(b)−L′​(a))4,\min\bigl\{u(z-a),\,v(b-z)\bigr\}\ \leq\ \frac{uv}{u+v}\,(b-a)\ \leq\ \frac{u+v}{4}\,(b-a)=\frac{(b-a)\bigl(L^{\prime}(b)-L^{\prime}(a)\bigr)}{4},

where the first inequality maximizes the minimum of an increasing and a decreasing linear function of zz, and the second uses 4​u​v≤(u+v)24uv\leq(u+v)^{2} (the gap is zero if u+v=0u+v=0). Since L′​(b)−L′​(a)=ΦN​(b)−ΦN​(a)≤ϕN​(0)​(b−a)L^{\prime}(b)-L^{\prime}(a)=\Phi_{N}(b)-\Phi_{N}(a)\leq\phi_{N}(0)(b-a), the gap is at most σ​(zi+1−zi)2​ϕN​(0)/4\sigma(z_{i+1}-z_{i})^{2}\phi_{N}(0)/4. Appendix B Notation

Appendix C Reproducibility

The code is available in spot/code/. The script spotsim.py contains the model, the planning program (21), the forecasts, and the plant. The script concept.py computes the examples of Sections 4, 5 and 6, writes Table 1 and the macros quoted in those sections, and draws Figs. 3, 5, 6, 7 and 8. The script run.py runs every simulation of Section 7, 510 weeks in all, in about fifteen minutes on a ten-core laptop. The script report.py converts its output into Table 3 and Figs. 9, 10, 11 and 12, and it writes every number quoted in Section 7. Linear programs are solved by HiGHS [16] through SciPy. The hour-of-day profile of interactive load is read from data/derived_hod_profile.json, which holds the mean share of daily token volume in each hour, computed from 30 days of hourly candles of a public inference marketplace [32]. The tier price ratios quoted in Section 2 are medians over the tiered endpoints in a snapshot of a model router’s public listings taken on 31 October 2026 [28]. No other external data are used.
